Label and roll-material feeding · QR labels, protective film, foam, tape and steel sheets on SMT mounters

Labels arrive on rolls. They should reach the mounter's nozzle like clockwork.
1 s per cycle. ±0.2 mm on X and Y. One plug onto any mounter.

The SLF100X is a label feeder engineered for SMT mounters and roll-type auxiliary materials. Paper labels, protective film, foam, double-sided tape, conductive adhesive, copper foil and steel sheets load onto a 3-inch core tray, strip from the liner by the documented roll-stripping method, and present themselves to the mounter nozzle at a repeatable ±0.2 mm on both axes. A 42-type stepper motor with threaded feeding runs a 1-second cycle; fibre optic sensing and four adjustable speed gears keep the pace honest. The 8-core aviation plug carries the IO handshake — or run it standalone.

01 — Why it matters

Every label placed by hand is a minute the mounter waits and a defect you must trace

QR-code labels for MES traceability, protective film, foam pads, double-sided tape, conductive adhesive, copper foil and steel stiffeners for FPCs — all of it still ships on rolls, and on many lines all of it is still applied by hand. A person peeling a label off a liner is slow, inconsistent and invisible on the capacity sheet; a mis-read QR code is a recall waiting to be found. The SLF100X turns that bench into a mounter step: the nozzle picks a label exactly like it picks a component, on the same cycle, with the same traceability.

01

Hand labeling is the hidden bottleneck

Every label placed by hand costs seconds the mounter could spend placing components. Multiply by labels per board and boards per day and the 'small' stickers decide your real output — and nobody logs it because the mounter was never the constraint.

02

Manual placement escapes errors

A person applying labels can invert them, mis-align them, or fatigue by hour six — and a QR code that does not scan breaks the traceability chain for the whole batch. The SLF100X presents one label at a time at a known position: X ±0.2 mm, Y ±0.2 mm, cycle after cycle.

03

Traceability demands a machine step

MES and customer audits want every board labelled, placed and recorded like any other component. When the label is fed by the machine at mounter speed with a published feeding rate of ≤0.5%, it stops being a craft and starts being a process step you can control.

02 — The method

From label roll to pick position in six repeatable moves

Label feeding looks simple until you try to do it at mounter speed: the material must strip cleanly from its liner, advance one label per cycle, and stop at the same place every time. The SLF100X sequences it into six steps, all documented in the product documents.

01

Load the roll

The label or film roll drops onto the 3-inch core tray — standard size, customizable for your supply. Maximum tray load is 3 kg, and the lower belt conveyor carries the waste liner away as the roll unwinds.

02

Strip the liner

The documented roll-stripping method peels the label stock away from its PET or paper liner at a defined angle. Liner width <60, <80 or <100 mm, thickness 0.05–0.08 mm — the strip geometry is what makes a clean pick possible.

03

Advance by thread

A 42-type stepper motor (up to 600 RPM) drives threaded feeding: positive, backlash-controlled advance instead of friction pushing. Four adjustable speed gears set the pace; the published cycle time is 1 second per feed.

04

Sense and position

Fibre optic sensing reads the label index — standard '1 in 1', with '1 in 12' optional for multi-column materials. Position is set three ways: X by limit adjustment, Y by software, Z by mechanical adjustment.

05

The nozzle picks

The mounter's own nozzle descends into the pick zone and lifts the leading label or film piece. Because presentation is repeatable to ±0.2 mm on X and Y, the pick works on cycle one and cycle fifty thousand — the machine treats the label like any other component.

06

Rewind the liner

As labels are consumed, the empty liner is taken away by the lower belt conveyor; an independent rewind motor is optional for continuous runs. The published feeding rate is ≤0.5% — one miss per two hundred feeds, at most.

Feeding method, drive and adjustment details are quoted from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Built around the roll — a stepper, a screw and a fibre

42-type stepper, up to 600 RPM

Threaded feeding driven by a stepper motor: positive advance with controlled deceleration, so the label stops where the programme says it stops — cycle after cycle, gear after gear.

Roll stripping presentation

The material is peeled from its liner before the pick, so the nozzle lifts a free label, not a label fighting its backing. This is what makes film, foam and sticky double-sided tape feedable at all.

ARM (STC32) or PLC control

Two documented control paths — an ARM (STC32) board or a PLC — so the feeder matches the control culture already on your floor, and the same four-delay discipline applies either way.

Three-axis position adjustment

X by limit adjustment, Y by software, Z by mechanical adjustment. Coarse geometry is set once per material family; fine Y moves live in the recipe, not in the wrench.

Fibre optic '1 in 1' to '1 in 12'

The standard fibre head reads one label per index; the optional '1 in 12' head supports multi-column rolls — single row and multiple columns, or multi-column expansion, as the specification sheet puts it.

Lower belt conveyor rewinding

The spent liner leaves by the lower belt conveyor as standard; an independent rewind motor is optional for long continuous runs. Either way, nothing pulls back against the strip geometry.

Four gears, one handshake — controls an operator actually uses

Four adjustable speed gears

The feeding speed is selectable in four gears so the pace can match the mounter's cycle rather than a fixed default. The published cycle time is 1 second per feed.

Feeding rate ≤ 0.5%, tested

The product documents publish a feeding rate of ≤0.5%, backed by a 500-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test — sustained performance figures, not showroom numbers.

Fibre optic index sensing

The fibre head reads each label index and tells the controller the material is present and positioned. The head is cleaned regularly with alcohol so dust never shifts the datum.

IO handshake with the mounter

Through the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug the feeder exchanges the ready/request handshake with the mounter — or runs standalone. All signals ride one cable; all power rides the same plug.

06 — Installation

Six moves from crate to first label

The product documents define the whole commissioning: mechanical install, utilities, roll loading, IO handshake, and the speed and position tune. Plan for minutes, not hours — and have label rolls on hand for the tuning run.

STEP 1 · Unbox and inspect

Check the body, stepper drive, fibre optic head, lower belt conveyor and 8-core aviation plug against the parts list. Confirm the strip geometry is clean and the liner path is clear.

STEP 2 · Seat on the mounter bank

Mount the feeder at the pick position on the mounter bank and lock it to the machine datum. The feeder must be locked firmly — a loose mount is the most common cause of placement drift.

STEP 3 · Connect air and power

0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean air to the inlet; 24 V DC to the aviation plug. Never short 24 V to 0 V, and keep the air dry — wet air on a strip path is a feeding-rate killer.

STEP 4 · Load the roll and thread the liner

Drop the roll onto the 3-inch core, strip the liner at the defined angle, and feed the waste liner onto the lower belt conveyor. Leave a clean leader so the first label indexes correctly.

STEP 5 · Wire the IO handshake

The 8-core plug carries power and the IO handshake: the mounter requests, the feeder presents, the nozzle picks. Run under machine control or standalone — both modes are documented.

STEP 6 · Tune gears and verify

Select the speed gear that matches the mounter cycle, set X limit / Y software / Z mechanical positions, then run the verification: 500 consecutive feeds with a feeding rate at or below 0.5% is the published acceptance picture.

ARTICLE 01Every PCB that ships without a traceability label is a recall waiting to happen

QR-code labels are how MES systems know what a board is and where it has been. Here is the five-minute audit that prices your manual labeling bench — and the escape it eventually lets through.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Every board that leaves a smart EMS factory carries a story: which panel it came from, which paste it saw, which oven it passed. The only thing that keeps that story readable is a small QR-code label — and on far too many lines, that label is applied by a person with their fingers.

Hand-applied labels are slow, variable and undocumented. A tired operator at hour six places a label 2 mm off; a mis-peeled sticker folds on itself; a batch label prints correctly but is applied to the wrong panel. None of these events reach your MES, because the bench was never a machine step. The recall, when it comes, starts exactly there.

Here is the five-minute audit. Pick your highest-volume board. Count the labels it must carry, time one hand placement with a phone stopwatch, and multiply by your monthly board volume. Then ask the second question: how many traceability escapes last quarter began at the labeling bench? The first number prices the labour; the second prices the risk.

Once the bench has a number, the alternative is simple to specify. The SLF100X locks onto the mounter bank, strips the liner, and presents paper labels to the machine's own nozzle at X ±0.2 mm and Y ±0.2 mm, one per second, four speed gears to match your cycle. The placement is done by the machine that already places every other component — so the label enters the same traceability record the board does.

The compounding part: once labels are machine-placed, they enter your normal planning world. Cycle counts become real, changeovers get logged, and the bench's variability leaves your quality conversations. The next product that ships with a QR code stops being a staffing problem — the feeder is already running.

Run the five-minute audit this week. Then send us the label size, the liner width and the number you found — info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 — and we will tell you, honestly, whether a label feeder pays for your mix or whether hand placement is still the right answer.

ARTICLE 02The 1-second cycle: how a label feeder matches your mounter's pace

Cycle time is a promise to the mounter. What 1 s per feed actually buys you, the four gears behind it, and the two failure modes when the label falls behind.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

There is a number printed on the SLF100X specification sheet that decides whether the feeder is invisible on your line or the reason your mounter idles: the cycle time. It is 1 second per feed, selectable across four speed gears.

Think about what the mounter actually asks of the feed path. Every cycle, the nozzle descends, takes a label, and expects the next label to be at the pick position, at the right height, peeled free of its liner, before it returns. If the feed path is slower than the head, the head waits. If it is faster but less accurate, the head mis-picks. Both failures cost the same money — they just wear different masks.

The reusable method is to compare two numbers, not one. Take your mounter's placement cycle and the number of labels per board. Multiply: that is the demand side. Now take the feeder's cycle time — 1 s per feed, four gears to tune it — and divide: that is the supply side. If supply is faster than demand, the feed path is never the constraint.

The SLF100X's figures are published alongside a feeding accuracy of ±0.2 mm on both axes and a feeding rate of ≤0.5%, backed by a 500-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test. Those two tests are what tell you the 1 s is a sustained rate, not a showroom figure: the aging test ran for two days, not two minutes.

Log the gear, the speed and the accuracy on your changeover card. The first time a new material arrives, you will know from the card whether the feed path can keep up before you commit the line.

Send us your mounter's cycle time and your label count per board. We will tell you honestly whether the 1-second cycle keeps up, or whether your mix wants a second feeder.

ARTICLE 03Foam, film, foil, tape: the four-letter problem manual labeling cannot solve

The materials that made this feeder necessary — why sticky, soft and conductive roll goods defeat hand placement, and what stripping changes.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Foam. Film. Foil. Tape. Four materials that start with F and end with frustration — and every EMS engineer who has watched a hand station apply them knows exactly why.

The problem is the materials themselves. Foam pads are thick and compressible, so a hand never presses them the same way twice. Protective film is statically clingy and wants to fold. Copper foil is thin enough to tear on a fingernail and conductive enough to short a joint if it folds. Double-sided tape is, by definition, sticky on both faces — which means it sticks to the glove, the bench, and the next board's wrong side. Hand placement of these materials is not a process; it is a negotiation.

The reusable method is to ask what the machine needs and give it exactly that: a free piece of material, presented at a known position, on a known cycle. That is what the roll-stripping method does. The liner is peeled away at a defined angle before the pick, so the nozzle lifts a released piece — not a piece fighting its backing. The SLF100X window covers liner <60, <80 and <100 mm wide at 0.05–0.08 mm thick, PET film or paper tape.

Inside that window the feeder handles the whole four-letter family: paper labels, protective film, foam, double-sided tape, conductive adhesive, copper foil and steel sheet, with material size from just over 3 mm up to the liner width. The 42-type stepper with threaded feeding stops each piece at X ±0.2 mm and Y ±0.2 mm, so the placement is repeatable in a way the bench never was.

Inventory your hand stations against that list. Most of the 'impossible to automate' materials were simply never offered a strip geometry and a stepper that stops where it is told.

Send us a sample roll of your worst material — foam, film, foil or tape. We will run it, photograph the presentation, and tell you honestly whether it feeds.

ARTICLE 04±0.2 mm on two axes: the placement spec that makes labels a component

A repeatable tuning method for label feeding — the three adjustments that keep presentation honest through a full shift.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

A label becomes a component the day its placement carries a tolerance. Before that, it is a craft. The tolerance that makes the difference on the SLF100X is ±0.2 mm — on both the X and the Y axis.

Why two axes? Because a QR code that is 2 mm off in Y still scans, until it overlaps a connector and the label curls. Because protective film that is 2 mm off in X still covers, until it misses the edge it was meant to seal. Placement errors are invisible at the bench and expensive at the customer. A stated two-axis accuracy is what lets you treat the label like every other placement: inspected by position, not by opinion.

The method the product documents encode is three adjustments, each doing one job. X is set by limit adjustment — the coarse geometry of the pick position. Y is set by software — the fine axis lives in the recipe, not in a wrench. Z is set by mechanical adjustment — how high the material stands for the nozzle to take it cleanly. Three controls, one repeatable presentation.

The fibre optic head is the quiet half of the system. The standard '1 in 1' head reads each label index and tells the controller the material is present and positioned; the optional '1 in 12' head extends the same discipline to multi-column rolls. A dusty fibre reads late, the presentation drifts, and the ±0.2 mm figure becomes fiction. Clean it regularly with alcohol — the cheapest maintenance contract you will ever sign.

Log the X limit, the Y software offset and the Z mechanical setting per material family on the changeover card. The first time a new label arrives, you will know from the card what to dial before you dial it.

If your material sits outside the smooth-and-accurate window — too heavy, too soft, too sticky — tell us what happens at the pick. That is exactly the case the one-month custom solution service exists for.

ARTICLE 05Your SMT line already has the nozzle — it just needs something new to pick

The mounter compatibility story: Fuji, Juki, Panasonic, Yamaha, Samsung, Siemens — one handshake, one plug, one more part type.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Here is a quiet truth about SMT lines: the mounter is already a labeling machine. It has a nozzle, a vision system, a placement program and a cycle. What it lacks is something new to pick.

Every factory floor we support runs Fuji, Juki, Panasonic, Yamaha, Samsung or Siemens equipment — and the SLF100X product documents name all six as compatibility targets. The interface is the one the mounter already speaks: an 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug carrying 24 V and the IO handshake, or standalone operation when the bank is busy. The mounter requests; the feeder presents; the nozzle takes the label and places it exactly like a component.

What changes when the label enters the program? Everything downstream. The placement is reported like any other pick — so your MES sees the QR label as a step with a timestamp, not a bench with a signature. The vision system that already checks component orientation can check the label. The spare-nozzle drawer already holds the tooling.

The reusable method is a three-line inventory. One: list every material your line applies by hand that ships on a liner roll. Two: mark which ones fall inside the published window — liner <60 / 80 / 100 mm, 0.05–0.08 mm thick, material from just over 3 mm up to the liner width. Three: hand that list to your mounter's programmer and ask what the placement costs in cycle time. The answer is usually smaller than the fear.

Once labels are program steps, new products that ship with a QR code, a film or a foam pad stop being a staffing problem. They are a program revision.

Tell us the mounter and the bank position. We will quote the interface variant and, if you want it, a sample feeding test on your own material before you commit.

ARTICLE 063 kg of roll material, 500 consecutive feeds: the capacity maths nobody checks

Tray load, liner width and the published feeding rate — how to size the roll supply before the line discovers your answer.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Capacity maths on a label feeder is boring — until the line stops mid-shift because nobody did it. Three numbers decide it: the tray load, the liner width, and the published feeding rate.

Start with the tray. The SLF100X takes a 3-inch roll core as standard — customizable when your supplier ships something else — and the tray carries a maximum of 3 kg of roll material. A 3 kg roll sounds endless until you weigh a day of labels: run the grams-per-meter of your material against your boards-per-shift and the roll change becomes a scheduled event, not a surprise.

Then the liner. The published window is <60, <80 or <100 mm wide at 0.05–0.08 mm thick, PET film or paper tape, with material size from just over 3 mm up to the liner width. Multi-column materials — single row and multiple columns, or multi-column expansion — raise the count of picks per meter, which is exactly why the optional '1 in 12' fibre head exists.

Finally the rate. The documents publish a feeding rate of ≤0.5% — at most one miss per two hundred feeds — and record a 500-consecutive-feed test plus a 48-hour aging test. Those are the numbers to put in your capacity plan: a 1-second cycle that survives two days of aging is a rate you can schedule against.

Do the three lines before you order, and log them on the changeover card. Roll weight per day, picks per meter, expected misses per shift. The feeder will keep the promises; the maths is what lets you plan around them.

Send us your roll specification — core, liner width, material weight per meter. We will size the tray, the gear and the rewind option with you before the line discovers the answer.

ARTICLE 07FPC reinforcement at mounter speed: the process step hiding in a label feeder

Steel sheets and copper foil on flexible circuits used to be a hand station. Here is what changes when the mounter places them.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Flexible circuits have a quiet process step that rarely appears on the SMT flow diagram: reinforcement. A steel sheet or a copper foil backing goes on the FPC to stiffen a connector zone or shield a bend — and on most lines it goes on by hand.

Hand-reinforcing is a small factory of its own. Someone peels the stiffener from its liner, aligns it by eye, presses it down, and hopes the adhesive wets evenly. Steel sheet does not forgive a 1 mm error; copper foil tears; the adhesive layer shows bubbles an hour later at test. The step is slow, the quality is variable, and the traceability is a signature on a traveler.

The method hiding in the label feeder is exactly the FPC problem, restated. The SLF100X product documents list steel sheet and copper foil among the applicable materials — the same roll-stripping presentation that frees a label from its liner frees a stiffener from its backing, and the same 42-type stepper with threaded feeding stops it at X ±0.2 mm and Y ±0.2 mm for the nozzle to take.

Once the stiffener is a pick-and-place, the mounter does what mounters do: place it on the program, check it with vision, report it to the MES. The robotic-arm variant in the documents extends the same logic to roll materials off the SMT line entirely — the feeder becomes a supply station for assembly cells, not just for mounters.

Map your FPC reinforcement against the published window: liner <60 / 80 / 100 mm, 0.05–0.08 mm thick, stiffener from just over 3 mm up to the liner width. If it fits, it is a machine step now.

Send us the stiffener drawing and the FPC panel. We will show you the feeding test, the tray configuration and the honest cycle cost of moving the step onto the mounter.

ARTICLE 08Before you automate labeling, run these four numbers

A payback method with your own volumes, your own time study and your own price — plus the three savings the method deliberately leaves out.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SLF100X SMT Label Feeder product document and the Label Feeder-SLF100X specification sheet.

Most payback conversations about small automation are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the labels per board, the boards per day, and the seconds per hand placement you measured yourself — not the number from a brochure, your number. Line two: what does the feeder actually take over? Be honest: it automates the repeatable placements, not the weird ones. Use the share your process really allows. Line three: your loaded wage and your working days. Line four: divide the quoted feeder price by the annual labour the first three lines freed. If the answer is under twelve months, this is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

The calculator on this page runs those four lines exactly, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — every money figure is typed in by you.

Now the three savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the traceability escapes a manual bench lets through — the mis-read QR code that turns one defect into a batch recall; the machine slot a dedicated feeder frees on a crowded bank; and the training cost of the bench itself, which is really the cost of every new hire learning your materials with their fingers.

Every factory that starts measuring labeled labour finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'consumables' or 'overtime'. The four lines make it visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a tray configuration — liner width, spare kit, tuning card — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this feeder raises

What materials can the SLF100X actually feed?
Anything that ships on a liner roll inside the published window: paper labels, protective film, foam, double-sided tape, conductive adhesive, copper foil and steel sheet, on liner <60 / 80 / 100 mm wide and 0.05–0.08 mm thick, PET film or paper tape. Material size runs from just over 3 mm up to the liner width. If your part ships on a label roll today, it is very likely inside the window — send a sample roll and we will confirm the presentation.
Which mounters does it fit?
The product documents name Fuji, Juki, Panasonic, Yamaha, Samsung and Siemens — all major mounter brands. The interface is the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug with the IO handshake, or standalone operation. Tell us the machine and the bank position and we quote the interface variant.
How fast can it feed? What throughput should I plan?
The published cycle time is 1 second per feed, selectable across four speed gears, with feeding accuracy of X ±0.2 mm and Y ±0.2 mm. The feed path presents labels faster than the nozzle takes them — throughput is set by the mounter's pick cycle, not the feeder. The documents also record a 500-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test.
What happens when a label misses?
The published feeding rate is ≤0.5% — at most one miss per two hundred feeds. Most misses are tuning, not hardware: strip angle wrong, liner thickness outside 0.05–0.08 mm, fibre head dirty, or speed gear faster than the material can stop. Clean the fibre head regularly with alcohol and re-verify with a 500-feed run after any material change.
What are the power and utility requirements?
24 V DC at 1.5 A average / 3 A peak, and 0.4–0.6 MPa dry clean compressed air. Both arrive through the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug and the standard air inlet. The family manuals are explicit: never short 24 V to 0 V.
How does the feeder talk to the mounter?
IO communication through the aviation plug, or standalone operation. The mounter requests, the feeder advances and presents, the nozzle picks — the same handshake rhythm used for components, so the label becomes a placement the machine can report on line by line.
How long does installation and changeover take?
Mounting is a seat-and-lock on the bank — minutes, with no shimming. A material changeover is dropping a new roll on the 3-inch core and recalling the gear and position settings. The full commissioning, including the 500-feed verification, is a same-shift job.
How do I get a quotation?
Send a photo of your labelled material, the liner width, the board volumes and your machine list to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a tray configuration, a spare part kit proposal and a price — usually within one working day, with a sample feeding test available before you commit.
